abstract: |
  We introduce `tidyfinance`, an [R]{.proglang} package on CRAN for the core data workflow in empirical asset pricing: downloading stock returns and financial statements, constructing sorting variables, forming quantile portfolios, and computing long-short factor returns. A unified `download_data()` interface covers WRDS (CRSP, Compustat), Ken French's Data Library, FRED, and further sources. Modular functions handle fiscal-year lagging, breakpoint computation, and portfolio aggregation; every construction choice has a documented default and can be varied independently, making pipelines transparent and reproducible. We illustrate the `tidyfinance` workflow with a risk factor library covering `{r} arrow::read_parquet("data/sorting_variable_information.parquet") |> nrow()` sorting variables across `{r} arrow::read_parquet("data/portfolio_sort_grid.parquet") |> nrow()` precomputed specifications. The library is accessible via an open-source API and an interactive dashboard at [factors.tidy-finance.org](https://factors.tidy-finance.org).

## Introduction: Constructing financial risk factors {#sec-intro}

:::{.callout-note}
Core contribution of the paper: `tidyfinance`, a modular, open-source library for reproducible workflows in empirical asset pricing. 
The relevant steps are a unified data access interface, modular functions for data processing, especially lagging, filtering and implementing portfolio sorts. A secondary contribution is the open-source factor library covering `{r} nrow(sorting_variable_information)` sorting variables across `{r} nrow(portfolio_sort_grid)` specifications. The library is available via an API and an interactive dashboard at [factors.tidy-finance.org](https://factors.tidy-finance.org). 

- Python is not primary focus of the paper. We mention `py-tidyfinance` in the very end of the introduction to highlight access to the factor library and once when we show how to use `download_data`. 
::: 

Factor returns drive empirical asset pricing tests, portfolio allocation, and performance attribution. Every series, however, embeds dozens of methodological choices: how breakpoints are set, whether portfolios are equal- or value-weighted, how delistings are handled, and which fiscal-year lag is applied. These choices are rarely standardized and almost never published with code. Researchers who reproduce or extend a factor series must reconstruct each pipeline from scratch, with no guarantee their choices match those of the original authors.

No widely adopted, transparent source standardizes factor construction. Current practice relies on informal publication of factor series without code or documented workflows, limiting reproducibility, comparability, and extension. Existing resources illustrate the gap: the French Data Library [@fama.2023] provides canonical factors but no code; the Open Source Asset Pricing Project [@chen.2022] focuses on replication; the global factor database [@jensen.2023] targets [Python]{.proglang} only. No unified, open-source alternative exists.

We introduce `tidyfinance`, a modular framework ([R]{.proglang} on CRAN, [Python]{.proglang} on PyPI) for reproducible factor construction. The library covers `{r} sorting_variable_information |> nrow()` sorting variables and `{r} portfolio_sort_grid |> nrow()` total specifications. We document and test every design choice (breakpoints, weighting, rebalancing, sample inclusion) and expose each as a configurable parameter.

The package implements an end-to-end pipeline: data acquisition from the Wharton Research Data Services (WRDS), Compustat, and other common providers; automated variable construction with standard lagging and cleaning routines; and portfolio aggregation with configurable sorting. A programmatic application programming interface (API) provides access to precomputed factor series with versioning and batch retrieval. Researchers using [python]{.proglang} access the same data download functions and factor library via `py-tidyfinance`. An interactive dashboard at [factors.tidy-finance.org](https://factors.tidy-finance.org) makes the library accessible without code. All software and workflows are publicly available to enable replication, sensitivity analysis, and extension.

@hou.2020 replicate 452 cross-sectional anomalies and find that most fail to survive out-of-sample, attributing failures in part to undocumented construction variation across studies. @chen.2022 respond by publishing code for 212 anomaly portfolios, but their library targets a fixed, documented set rather than a reconfigurable pipeline. @jensen.2023 provide a global factor database without an open construction workflow. `tidyfinance` fills the gap all three leave open: every construction decision is explicit, configurable, and version-controlled, so researchers can trace and vary any assumption systematically.

Among [R]{.proglang} packages for quantitative finance, [tidyquant]{.pkg} [@dancho.2026], [PerformanceAnalytics]{.pkg} [@peterson.2026], and [quantmod]{.pkg} [@ryan.2025] support time-series retrieval and portfolio performance analytics. None begins at raw accounting and return data, applies the cleaning and lagging conventions factor construction requires, or exposes construction choices as configurable parameters. `tidyfinance` provides this upstream pipeline with a consistent API across both languages. Hence, it enables researchers to access standardized factor series without rebuilding data workflows in each environment.

### Installation and setup {#sec-installation}

You can install the released version of `tidyfinance` [from CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=tidyfinance) via:

```{r}
#| label: install-tidyfinance-cran
#| eval: false
install.packages("tidyfinance")
```

To install the development version of `tidyfinance` from [GitHub](https://github.com/tidy-finance/r-tidyfinance), first install the [pak]{.pkg} package if needed, then install the development version:

```{r}
#| label: install-tidyfinance-dev
#| eval: false
pak::pak("tidy-finance/r-tidyfinance")
```


### Design and workflow {#sec-design}

`tidyfinance` organises the empirical asset pricing workflow into three stages: data acquisition, variable construction, and portfolio sorting. Each stage involves dozens of small decisions, such as universe filters, cleaning rules, rebalancing conventions, and breakpoint definitions. These decisions are rarely documented uniformly across studies, making replication difficult. @fig-workflow-diagram shows the pipeline and the package functions at each stage. The functions expose documented defaults that follow established conventions and configurable parameters where reasonable researchers might disagree. In this way, researchers can adopt the full pipeline or call individual functions within their own workflows.^[A companion Python package `tidyfinance` provides the same interface with identical function signatures and dataset identifiers, so analyses can be ported between the two languages without changes to the data layer.]

```{mermaid}

%%| fig-cap: "Research workflow for factor construction with `tidyfinance`, illustrating the three-stage pipeline and the package functions involved at each step."
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'rankSpacing': 30, 'padding': 15}, 'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '9x'}}}%%

flowchart LR
    A("<b>Data acquisition</b><br/><br/><code>download_data()</code><br/><br/><br/>")
    --> B("<b>Variable construction</b><br/><br/><code>add_lagged_columns()</code><br/><code>join_lagged_values()</code><br/><br/>")
    --> C("<b>Portfolio returns</b><br/><br/><code>compute_breakpoints()</code><br/><code>assign_portfolio()</code><br/><code>compute_portfolio_returns()</code>")
```

`download_data()` applies standard cleaning conventions automatically. For CRSP monthly data (version 2), the function restricts the universe to common equity securities traded on NYSE, AMEX, or NASDAQ. It computes market capitalisation as shares outstanding times price, constructs a one-month lag for portfolio weights, and maps exchange codes and SIC codes to readable labels. Excess returns are raw returns minus the Fama-French risk-free rate; observations with missing returns or market capitalisation are dropped. CRSP version 2 incorporates delisting returns directly, eliminating the need for a separate adjustment.

For Compustat annual data, `download_data()` restricts to industrial-format consolidated statements and retains only the most recent observation per firm-year. It constructs book equity through a coalesce hierarchy: stockholders' equity, then common equity plus preferred stock, then total assets minus total liabilities. The function adjusts for deferred taxes and investment tax credits and subtracts preferred stock.

All datasets returned by `download_data()` use a single `date` column that follows the same rules across frequencies. Daily observations return the trading date. Monthly observations are dated to the last calendar day of the reference month, regardless of whether that day was a trading day. Quarterly and annual observations take the fiscal period-end date as reported by the original source; for Compustat, this is the firm's fiscal year-end (`datadate`), which can differ from December across firms and across years for the same firm. Macroeconomic series from FRED keep their original release dates. A simple equality join on `date` therefore aligns observations of the same frequency, while cross-frequency joins, such as merging monthly returns with annual fundamentals, require the lagging logic described in the next subsection.

### Variable construction {#sec-variable-construction}

Most predictive variables in asset pricing studies are based on lagged information so that portfolio formation in month $t$ should always use only data observable at the end of month $t-1$. `add_lagged_columns()` automates this. For each row in the data, it looks back over a configurable window and attaches the most recent observed value of the chosen columns. By default (`ff_adjustment = FALSE`), the window is bounded by `lag` (the minimum delay between observation and use) and `max_lag` (the maximum delay before a stale value is treated as missing). Within this window, the function picks the most recent non-missing value; if no observation falls in the window, the lagged column takes `NA`.

A second mode, enabled by `ff_adjustment = TRUE`, implements the Fama-French convention [@fama.1993]. Accounting variables for fiscal year $t-1$ are assumed to become public information by June of year $t$ and are then used for portfolio formation from July of $t$ through June of $t+1$. This produces step-function lagged values that update once per year at the June/July boundary, regardless of the underlying fiscal year-end. @fig-lagging-illustration contrasts the two mechanisms. The upper panel shows a standard look-back window controlled by `lag` and `max_lag`. The lower panel implements the Fama-French convention: fiscal-year data from year $t-1$ becomes available only from July of year $t$, so all months from July through June share the same lagged value locked in at the previous rebalancing. In both cases, `add_lagged_columns()` selects the most recent observed value within the window.

`join_lagged_values()` is a related helper that merges lagged values from one data frame into another using the same windowing logic. It is useful when the target panel and the source panel are at different frequencies, for example when joining monthly accounting data into a quarterly target panel. The function takes the same `ff_adjustment` argument as `add_lagged_columns()`, so the Fama-French convention can be applied at the join step rather than as a separate transformation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-lagging-illustration
#| fig-cap: "Two lagging mechanisms in `add_lagged_columns()`. Each row represents a data series with observed (filled) and missing (hollow) cells. Dashed rectangles mark the search window; arrows show which value gets matched to each target month."
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| echo: false
library(ggforce)

ts <- 0.94
corner <- unit(4, "pt")


# Extra padding so the dashed box extends slightly beyond the tiles
win_pad <- 0.15

# Extend data back by one month (Nov Y-2) so Year T-2 has a real bracket span
month_labels <- month.abb[c(11, 12, 1:12, 1:7)]
n <- length(month_labels)

x_labels <- -0.8
x_ff <- 0.55
x_std <- 3.0

obs_pattern <- c(
  FALSE, #  1  Nov Y-2
  TRUE, #  2  Dec Y-2  (fiscal year-end Y-2)
  FALSE, #  3  Jan Y-1
  FALSE, #  4  Feb Y-1
  FALSE, #  5  Mar Y-1
  FALSE, #  6  Apr Y-1
  TRUE, #  7  May Y-1
  FALSE, #  8  Jun Y-1
  FALSE, #  9  Jul Y-1
  TRUE, # 10  Aug Y-1
  FALSE, # 11  Sep Y-1
  TRUE, # 12  Oct Y-1
  FALSE, # 13  Nov Y-1
  TRUE, # 14  Dec Y-1  (fiscal year-end Y-1)
  TRUE, # 15  Jan Y
  FALSE, # 16  Feb Y
  TRUE, # 17  Mar Y
  FALSE, # 18  Apr Y
  TRUE, # 19  May Y
  FALSE, # 20  Jun Y
  TRUE # 21  Jul Y
)

df_data <- data.frame(
  y = 1:n,
  label = month_labels,
  observed = obs_pattern,
  # Data recency: older months fade toward transparent, newer ones solid
  alpha = 0.35 + 0.65 * ((1:n) / n)
)

obs <- df_data[df_data$observed, ]
miss <- df_data[!df_data$observed, ]

# Target is Jul Y (position 21). With lag = months(7), max_lag = months(18):
# Search window = [target - max_lag, target - lag] = [3, 14] = Jan Y-1 to Dec Y-1
# Note: Nov Y-2 (pos 1) and Dec Y-2 (pos 2) are OUTSIDE the window.
std_win_left <- 3
std_win_right <- 14
target <- 21

# Standard: most recent observed in [3, 14]
# Observed in window: 7, 10, 12, 14 -> most recent = 14 (Dec Y-1)
std_matched <- 14

ff_win_left <- 3
ff_win_right <- 14
ff_matched <- 14

tiles <- function(rows, cx, grp_offset = 0, xsize = ts) {
  do.call(
    rbind,
    lapply(seq_len(nrow(rows)), function(i) {
      data.frame(
        x = cx + c(-1, 1, 1, -1) * xsize / 2,
        y = rows$y[i] + c(-1, -1, 1, 1) * ts / 2,
        group = grp_offset + i,
        alpha = if ("alpha" %in% names(rows)) rows$alpha[i] else NA_real_
      )
    })
  )
}

grp_obs1 <- n
grp_miss1 <- n + nrow(obs)
grp_obs2 <- n + nrow(obs) + nrow(miss)
grp_miss2 <- n + nrow(obs) + nrow(miss) + nrow(obs)

obs1_poly <- tiles(obs, x_std, grp_obs1)
miss1_poly <- tiles(miss, x_std, grp_miss1)
obs2_poly <- tiles(obs, x_ff, grp_obs2)
miss2_poly <- tiles(miss, x_ff, grp_miss2)

# --- Standard grey arrows ----------------------------------------------------
# For each target t in 12..20, find most recent observed in [t-18, t-7]
# Observed positions: 2, 7, 10, 12, 14, 15, 17, 19, 21
# t=20: window [2,13], obs in window: 2,7,10,12   -> 12
# t=19: window [1,12], obs in window: 2,7,10,12   -> 12
# t=18: window [1,11], obs in window: 2,7,10      -> 10
# t=17: window [1,10], obs in window: 2,7,10      -> 10
# t=16: window [1,9],  obs in window: 2,7         -> 7
# t=15: window [1,8],  obs in window: 2,7         -> 7
# t=14: window [1,7],  obs in window: 2,7         -> 7
# t=13: window [1,6],  obs in window: 2           -> 2
# t=12: window [1,5],  obs in window: 2           -> 2
std_grey <- data.frame(
  y = c(20, 19, 18, 17, 16, 15, 14, 13, 12),
  yend = c(12, 12, 10, 10, 7, 7, 7, 2, 2)
)

# --- FF grey arrows ----------------------------------------------------------
# FF candidates (last observed per year): Dec Y-2 (pos 2), Dec Y-1 (pos 14)
# For targets before Jul Y, only Dec Y-2 is in range -> all point to pos 2.
# Jul Y (target) is the first month where Dec Y-1 enters the window -> pos 14.
ff_grey <- data.frame(
  y = c(20, 19, 18, 17, 16, 15, 14, 13, 12),
  yend = c(2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2)
)

ggplot() +
  # Month timeline: horizontal line with tick marks
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x_labels,
    xend = x_labels,
    y = 0.5,
    yend = n + 0.5,
    color = "grey40",
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x_labels - 0.08,
    xend = x_labels + 0.08,
    y = 1:n,
    yend = 1:n,
    color = "grey40",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  # Month labels — just below the axis tick line
  geom_text(
    data = df_data,
    aes(x = x_labels - 0.2, y = y, label = label),
    size = 4,
    color = "grey40",
    hjust = 0.5
  ) +
  # --- Standard column: observed ---------------------------------------------
  geom_shape(
    data = obs1_poly,
    aes(x = x, y = y, group = group, alpha = alpha),
    fill = tf_dark_blue,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    radius = corner
  ) +
  geom_shape(
    data = miss1_poly,
    aes(x = x, y = y, group = group),
    fill = "grey97",
    color = "grey80",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    radius = corner
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = miss,
    aes(x = x_std, y = y),
    label = "NA",
    size = 3.2,
    color = "grey65",
    fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  # --- FF column: observed ---------------------------------------------------
  geom_shape(
    data = obs2_poly,
    aes(x = x, y = y, group = group, alpha = alpha),
    fill = tf_dark_blue,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    radius = corner
  ) +
  geom_shape(
    data = miss2_poly,
    aes(x = x, y = y, group = group),
    fill = "grey97",
    color = "grey80",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    radius = corner
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = miss,
    aes(x = x_ff, y = y),
    label = "NA",
    size = 3.2,
    color = "grey65",
    fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  # --- Standard grey arrows --------------------------------------------------
  geom_curve(
    data = data.frame(
      x = x_std + ts / 2,
      xend = x_std + ts / 2,
      y = std_grey$y,
      yend = std_grey$yend + 0.15
    ),
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    curvature = -0.2,
    color = "grey70",
    alpha = 0.5,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.08, "cm"), type = "closed"),
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  # Standard search window
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = x_std - ts / 2 - win_pad,
    xmax = x_std + ts / 2 + win_pad,
    ymin = std_win_left - ts / 2 - win_pad,
    ymax = std_win_right + ts / 2 + win_pad,
    fill = NA,
    color = tf_yellow,
    linewidth = 0.9,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x_std - ts / 2 - win_pad - 0.2,
    y = c(std_win_left - ts / 2 - win_pad, std_win_right + ts / 2 + win_pad),
    label = c("max_lag", "lag"),
    color = tf_yellow,
    size = 3.4,
    fontface = "italic",
    hjust = -0.2,
    vjust = 0.5
  ) +
  # Standard highlighted arrow: Jul Y -> Dec Y-1
  annotate(
    "curve",
    x = x_std + ts / 2,
    xend = x_std + ts / 2,
    y = target,
    yend = std_matched + 0.2,
    curvature = -0.2,
    color = tf_dark_blue,
    linewidth = 0.9,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.14, "cm"), type = "closed")
  ) +
  # --- FF grey arrows --------------------------------------------------------
  geom_curve(
    data = data.frame(
      x = x_ff + ts / 2,
      xend = x_ff + ts / 2,
      y = ff_grey$y,
      yend = ff_grey$yend + 0.15
    ),
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    curvature = -0.2,
    color = "grey70",
    alpha = 0.5,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.08, "cm"), type = "closed"),
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  # FF search window
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = x_ff - ts / 2 - win_pad,
    xmax = x_ff + ts / 2 + win_pad,
    ymin = ff_win_left - ts / 2 - win_pad,
    ymax = ff_win_right + ts / 2 + win_pad,
    fill = NA,
    color = tf_yellow,
    linewidth = 0.9,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x_ff - ts / 2 - win_pad - 0.2,
    y = c(ff_win_left - ts / 2 - win_pad, ff_win_right + ts / 2 + win_pad),
    label = c("max_lag", "lag"),
    color = tf_yellow,
    size = 3.4,
    fontface = "italic",
    hjust = -0.2,
    vjust = 0.5
  ) +
  # FF highlighted arrow: Jul Y -> Dec Y-1
  annotate(
    "curve",
    x = x_ff + ts / 2,
    xend = x_ff + ts / 2,
    y = target,
    yend = ff_matched + 0.2,
    curvature = -0.2,
    color = tf_dark_blue,
    linewidth = 0.9,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.14, "cm"), type = "closed")
  ) +
  # --- Main title (bold) -----------------------------------------------------
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = max(x_std, x_ff) + ts / 2 + 1.0,
    y = n / 2,
    label = "data |> add_lagged_columns(lag = months(7), max_lag = months(18))",
    color = "black",
    size = 4.5,
    family = "mono",
    fontface = "bold",
    hjust = 0.5
  ) +
  # --- Panel labels (left margin, rotated, two lines, bold) ------------------
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x_std,
    y = -0.1,
    label = "ff_adjustment\n= FALSE",
    color = "grey30",
    size = 4.0,
    family = "mono",
    fontface = "bold",
    angle = 90,
    hjust = 0.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    lineheight = 0.9
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x_ff,
    y = -0.1,
    label = "ff_adjustment\n= TRUE",
    color = "grey30",
    size = 4.0,
    family = "mono",
    fontface = "bold",
    angle = 90,
    hjust = 0.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    lineheight = 0.9
  ) +
  # --- Year-change dashed lines (SHORTENED) ----------------------------------
  # Now stop at the right edge of the yellow search window rather than extending
  # all the way across to the title area. This removes the long dashes cluttering
  # the top of the figure.
  # Between Dec Y-2 (pos 2) and Jan Y-1 (pos 3): line at 2.5
  # Between Dec Y-1 (pos 14) and Jan Y (pos 15): line at 14.5
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x_labels - 0.55,
    xend = x_std + ts / 2 + 0.7,
    y = 2.5,
    yend = 2.5,
    color = "grey30",
    linewidth = 0.5,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x_labels - 0.55,
    xend = x_std + ts / 2 + 0.7,
    y = 14.5,
    yend = 14.5,
    color = "grey30",
    linewidth = 0.5,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  # --- Year span brackets ----------------------------------------------------
  # Year T-2:  pos 1 to 2   (Nov-Dec Y-2)
  # Year T-1:  pos 3 to 14  (Jan-Dec Y-1)
  # Year T:    pos 15 to 21 (Jan-Jul Y)
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x_labels - 0.55,
    xend = x_labels - 0.55,
    y = c(1, 3, 15),
    yend = c(2, 14, 21),
    color = "grey30",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  # Bracket end caps
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x_labels - 0.50,
    xend = x_labels - 0.60,
    y = c(1, 2, 3, 14, 15, 21),
    yend = c(1, 2, 3, 14, 15, 21),
    color = "grey30",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  # Year labels at midpoints:
  # Year T-2: midpoint of [1, 2] = 1.5
  # Year T-1: midpoint of [3, 14] = 8.5
  # Year T:   midpoint of [15, 21] = 18
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x_labels - 0.75,
    y = c(1.5, 8.5, 18),
    label = c("Year T-2", "Year T-1", "Year T"),
    color = "grey30",
    size = 4.0,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_alpha_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(x_labels - 1.15, max(x_std, x_ff) + ts / 2 + 1.3),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(-1.0, n + 0.55),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(5, 10, 5, 10))
```

A handful of additional helpers cover routine operations that recur across empirical studies. `winsorize()` and `trim()` handle outliers in cross-sectional variables: the former replaces values beyond user-specified quantiles with the quantile values themselves, while the latter sets them to `NA`. `estimate_model()` fits a linear model from a formula string and returns the coefficients as a tidy one-row data frame, which composes naturally with `group_by()` for grouped or rolling regressions such as time-series factor exposures. `compute_rolling_value()` applies an arbitrary aggregation function over a rolling window defined in calendar time rather than row counts, accommodating irregular observation frequencies and missing periods.

### Portfolio sorting {#sec-portfolio-sorting}

Portfolio sorts are among the most widely used tools in empirical asset pricing [@bali.2016]. The procedure groups stocks each period into portfolios based on a sorting variable, such as size, beta, book-to-market, or momentum, and then compares return distributions across the resulting portfolios. The long-short return between the extreme portfolios is interpreted as a factor-mimicking strategy and serves as the basis for tests of whether the sorting variable forecasts future returns. We expose the procedure through four composable functions.

`compute_breakpoints()` takes a cross-section and a sorting variable and returns the numeric cutoffs that define the portfolio boundaries. The user supplies either a number of portfolios (for example, five for quintiles) or an explicit vector of percentiles, but not both. A `breakpoints_exchanges` argument restricts the universe used to compute breakpoints. The standard convention is NYSE-only, which prevents the large cross-section of small NASDAQ firms from dominating the lower bins. A related `breakpoints_min_size_threshold` argument excludes stocks below a market-cap quantile from the breakpoint computation, which is useful for size-related sorts where microcaps would otherwise distort the cutoffs. A `smooth_bunching` flag handles cases where the sorting variable clusters at the edges by pinning extreme values to the boundary portfolios and recomputing breakpoints on the remainder.

`assign_portfolio()` maps each observation to a portfolio integer using the breakpoints. The breakpoint computation is delegated to a user-supplied function (defaulting to `compute_breakpoints()`), so custom rules such as dollar-based cutoffs or industry-adjusted breakpoints can be plugged in without rewriting the assignment logic. In practice, `assign_portfolio()` is called separately for each rebalancing date, so that portfolios are reformed each period rather than fixed once for the whole sample.

`compute_portfolio_returns()` ties the lower-level pieces together into a single call. Given a panel of stock data, one or two sorting variables, a sorting method, and `breakpoint_options`, it handles rebalancing, breakpoint computation, portfolio assignment, and return aggregation. It then returns a complete panel of portfolio returns. For each portfolio-date the function reports three return measures: equal-weighted, value-weighted using `mktcap_lag` as the weight, and capped value-weighted. The capped version pulls weights above the `cap_weight` percentile (default 0.8) back to that cap, which prevents a small number of megacap firms from dominating the portfolio. A `min_portfolio_size` argument sets the minimum number of constituents below which the corresponding return is set to `NA`. An optional `rebalancing_month` argument switches from period-by-period rebalancing to annual rebalancing in the specified month. Portfolios formed in that month are then held constant for the following twelve months.

The function supports three sorting schemes, illustrated in @fig-illustrate-portfolio-helper. A *univariate* sort uses a single variable. An *independent bivariate* sort computes breakpoints on each variable separately and intersects the resulting bins to produce a two-way grid. A *dependent bivariate* sort first partitions the cross-section by the secondary (control) variable and then re-sorts within each bucket on the main variable, which is the appropriate choice when the second variable is treated as a control rather than as an independent dimension of variation. For bivariate sorts, returns are averaged over the secondary variable so that only the main-variable portfolios are returned.

```{r}
#| label: illustrate-portfolio-helper
#| echo: false
set.seed(3010)

n <- 1000
rho <- 0.6

# shared signal
f <- rnorm(n)

# independent noise
e1 <- rnorm(n)
e2 <- rnorm(n)

# construct correlated latent variables
x1 <- f + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * e1
x2 <- f + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * e2

# map to (0,1)
asset_growth <- pnorm(x1)
mktcap_lag <- pnorm(x2)

cross_section <- data.frame(asset_growth, mktcap_lag)
n_portfolio <- 2

breakpoints_ag <- cross_section |>
  compute_breakpoints(
    "asset_growth",
    breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)
  )

portfolios_univariate <- cross_section |>
  mutate(
    ag_portfolio = assign_portfolio(
      pick(everything()),
      "asset_growth",
      breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)
    )
  )

portfolios_independent <- cross_section |>
  mutate(
    ag_portfolio = assign_portfolio(
      pick(everything()),
      "asset_growth",
      breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)
    ),
    size_portfolio = assign_portfolio(
      pick(everything()),
      "mktcap_lag",
      breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)
    ),
    portfolio_cell = paste0(ag_portfolio, "-", size_portfolio)
  )

portfolios_dependent <- cross_section |>
  mutate(
    ag_portfolio = assign_portfolio(
      pick(everything()),
      "asset_growth",
      breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(ag_portfolio) |>
  mutate(
    size_portfolio = assign_portfolio(
      pick(everything()),
      "mktcap_lag",
      breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)
    ),
    portfolio_cell = paste0(ag_portfolio, "-", size_portfolio)
  ) |>
  ungroup()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-illustrate-portfolio-helper
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Portfolio sort approaches illustrated for a single month (December 2024). Each panel plots stock-month observations assigned to `{r} n_portfolio`×`{r} n_portfolio` portfolios based on asset growth rank (x-axis) and size rank (y-axis), both expressed as percentiles. Colors indicate portfolio cell assignment. The univariate sort (left) assigns portfolios on asset growth alone; the independent bivariate sort (center) assigns each dimension independently; the dependent bivariate sort (right) sorts on size first, then on asset growth within size groups."
common_theme <- list(
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent,
    breaks = breakpoints_ag,
    expand = c(0.01, 0)
  ),
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = c(0.01, 0)),
  labs(x = "Asset growth rank", y = "Size rank"),
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
  )
)

p1 <- portfolios_univariate |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = asset_growth,
    y = mktcap_lag,
    color = as.factor(ag_portfolio)
  )) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Univariate sort") +
  common_theme

p2 <- portfolios_independent |>
  ggplot(aes(x = asset_growth, y = mktcap_lag, color = portfolio_cell)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Independent bivariate sort") +
  common_theme

p3 <- portfolios_dependent |>
  ggplot(aes(x = asset_growth, y = mktcap_lag, color = portfolio_cell)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Dependent bivariate sort") +
  common_theme

p1 +
  p2 +
  p3 +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Portfolio sort approaches",
    subtitle = glue::glue(
      "December 2024 — {n_portfolio}×{n_portfolio} portfolios"
    ),
    theme = theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot"
    )
  )
```

`compute_long_short_returns()` is a thin convenience layer that takes the output of `compute_portfolio_returns()` and computes the spread between the top and bottom portfolios. A `direction` argument controls the sign and defaults to `"top_minus_bottom"`. The function returns one long-short series per return measure available in the input, so the equal-weighted, value-weighted, and capped value-weighted spreads are produced in a single call. This is the long-short factor-mimicking return that is usually the object of interest in the asset-pricing literature.

## Vignette: A case study in factor construction {#sec-ag}

:::{.callout-note}
This section shows the workflow from scratch without excessive documentation by going through data aggregation, variable construction for asset growth, lagging and sorting into portfolios. The purpose is to illustrate the workflow and the relevant functions in a concrete example. We do not show every step of the data cleaning process for brevity.

- Compute asset growth risk factor time series once with defaults (describe the defaults) using `implement_portfolio_sort()`.
- use the `filter_options`, `breakpoint_options`, and other arguments to streamline the process for an *exotic* example.
- Illustrate "standard" summary stats for one specification of the factor or use fama-mac beth functionality for some standard testing.
::: 

We walk through the construction of the asset growth factor from raw CRSP and Compustat data to long-short portfolio returns, implementing each stage of @fig-workflow-diagram in turn. Each step uses a `tidyfinance` function and generalises directly to any sorting variable in the factor library.^[Installation of the `tidyfinance` package is described in the appendix in  @sec-installation Installation and setup.]

Once installed, load `tidyfinance` and a minimal set of packages for data manipulation and visualisation.

```{r}
#| label: load-tidyfinance
library("tidyfinance")
```

```{r}
#| label: load-libraries
#| message: false
library("dplyr")
library("tidyr")
library("lubridate")
```

### Data download {#sec-data-download}

Before the first WRDS download, call `set_wrds_credentials()` to store WRDS credentials securely in `.Renviron`; subsequent `download_data()` calls establish the database connection automatically.

```{r}
#| label: set-date-range
date_start <- as.Date("1960-01-01")
date_end <- as.Date("2024-12-31")
```

```{r}
#| label: load-crsp-compustat
#| echo: false
crsp_monthly <- arrow::read_parquet("data/crsp_monthly.parquet")
compustat_annual <- arrow::read_parquet("data/compustat_annual.parquet")
```

First, we download monthly stock returns from CRSP. Setting `add_ccm_links = TRUE` appends CRSP-Compustat linking identifiers needed to merge with financial statement data in the next step.

```{r}
#| label: download-crsp
#| eval: false
crsp_monthly <- download_data(
  domain = "wrds",
  dataset = "crsp_monthly",
  version = "v2",
  start_date = date_start,
  end_date = date_end,
  add_ccm_links = TRUE
)
```

The dataset contains `{r} nrow(crsp_monthly)` stock-month observations for `{r} length(unique(crsp_monthly$permno))` unique stocks, covering the period from `{r} min(crsp_monthly$date)` to `{r} max(crsp_monthly$date)`.

Next, we download annual financial statements from Compustat.

```{r}
#| label: download-compustat
#| eval: false
compustat_annual <- download_data(
  domain = "wrds",
  dataset = "compustat_annual",
  start_date = date_start,
  end_date = date_end,
  additional_columns = c("at", "ib"),
  only_us = TRUE
)
```

Annual Compustat data contains `{r} nrow(compustat_annual)` firm-year observations for `{r} length(unique(compustat_annual$gvkey))` unique firms, covering the period from `{r} min(compustat_annual$date)` to `{r} max(compustat_annual$date)`. The `additional_columns` argument retrieves total assets (`at`) and income before extraordinary items (`ib`), needed for computing asset growth and applying an earnings filter in later steps. Setting `only_us = TRUE` restricts the dataset to USD-denominated observations, ensuring consistency with CRSP.

### Data cleaning and variable construction {#sec-data-cleaning}

We illustrate data cleaning and variable construction using asset growth (AG) as our running example. Asset growth is the year-over-year percentage change in total assets [@cooper.2008], 
$$
AG_t = (AT_t - AT_{t-1}) / AT_{t-1}.
$$

The `add_lagged_columns()` function from `tidyfinance` handles temporal alignment by creating a lagged version of total assets grouped by firm identifier (`gvkey`) with a one-year lag. Non-finite values (arising when lagged total assets are zero or missing) become `NA`.^[For the sake of simplicity we do not show every step of the data cleaning process in the paper. For instance, we apply an earnings filter to exclude firms with negative or zero income before extraordinary items (`ib`), which is a common practice in the literature to mitigate the influence of financial distress on asset growth portfolios. This filter is implemented in the code but not shown in the paper for brevity. We also apply an age filter to exclude firms younger than two years, which is common in the literature to ensure that the sorting variable is based on stable financial information. This filter is also implemented in the code but not shown in the paper for brevity. The factor library API provides preprocessed panels with all these filters applied, so users can access the final sorting variables without having to implement these steps themselves.] 

```{r}
#| label: compute-sorting-variables
sorting_variable_data <- compustat_annual |>
  add_lagged_columns(
    "at",
    lag = years(1),
    by = "gvkey",
  ) |>
  mutate(
    asset_growth = (at - at_lag) / at_lag,
    asset_growth = if_else(is.finite(asset_growth), asset_growth, NA_real_)
  ) |>
  select(gvkey, date, asset_growth)
```

`sorting_variable_data` contains one observation per firm-year, the natural unit for cross-sectional analysis of annual accounting variables. The package provides `filter_out()` as a convenience wrapper that removes rows matching a logical predicate, and `winsorize()` to clip numeric vectors at specified quantile bounds. Asset growth is heavily right-skewed: a small number of firms with dramatic balance-sheet expansions generate extreme positive values. We winsorize at the 1st and 99th percentiles before computing summary statistics. @tbl-ag-summary reports the pooled cross-sectional summary; @tbl-ag-summary-yearly shows how those moments vary across calendar years.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ag-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Cross-sectional summary statistics for asset growth (winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles). The table reports the number of firm-year observations (N), the mean, standard deviation (SD), and selected percentiles of the annual asset growth distribution computed from `sorting_variable_data`."
#| echo: false
sorting_variable_data |>
  filter_out(is.na(asset_growth)) |>
  mutate(asset_growth = winsorize(asset_growth, 0.01)) |>
  summarise(
    N = n(),
    Mean = mean(asset_growth),
    SD = sd(asset_growth),
    P10 = quantile(asset_growth, 0.10),
    P25 = quantile(asset_growth, 0.25),
    Median = median(asset_growth),
    P75 = quantile(asset_growth, 0.75),
    P90 = quantile(asset_growth, 0.90)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ag-summary-yearly
#| tbl-cap: "Time-series averages of annual cross-sectional summary statistics for asset growth (winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles). For each calendar year, cross-sectional mean, standard deviation, and median are computed from `sorting_variable_data`; the table reports the time-series mean, minimum, and maximum of those annual statistics."
#| echo: false
sorting_variable_data |>
  filter_out(is.na(asset_growth)) |>
  group_by(year = year(date)) |>
  mutate(
    p01 = quantile(asset_growth, 0.01),
    p99 = quantile(asset_growth, 0.99),
    asset_growth = pmax(pmin(asset_growth, p99), p01)
  ) |>
  summarise(
    N = n(),
    Mean = mean(asset_growth),
    SD = sd(asset_growth),
    Median = median(asset_growth),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  summarise(
    Years = n(),
    `Avg N` = round(mean(N)),
    `Mean (avg)` = mean(Mean),
    `Mean (min)` = min(Mean),
    `Mean (max)` = max(Mean),
    `SD (avg)` = mean(SD),
    `Median (avg)` = mean(Median),
    `Median (min)` = min(Median),
    `Median (max)` = max(Median)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The next step merges annual sorting variables onto the monthly CRSP stock panel using `join_lagged_values()`. The function aligns fiscal-year-end data with monthly observations through a configurable lag window. Setting `ff_adjustment = TRUE` implements the Fama-French convention [@fama.1993], aligning fiscal-year data from year $t$ with portfolio formation in July of year $t+1$ through a 12-to-18-month look-back window. The same lagging process generalizes to all sorting variables in the full factor library. The factor library API provides precomputed lagged panels for all variables.

With both lagging mechanisms documented, we apply `join_lagged_values()` to merge the sorting variable onto the monthly return panel. @fig-ag-percentiles shows the 33rd, 50th, and 66th percentiles of asset growth over time in the resulting panel; pronounced spikes during economic expansions and contractions highlight the cyclical nature of corporate investment that portfolio sorts aim to exploit.

```{r}
#| label: lag-sorting-variables
#| cache: true
sorting_data <- crsp_monthly |>
  join_lagged_values(
    sorting_variable_data,
    "gvkey",
    min_lag = months(7),
    max_lag = months(18),
    ff_adjustment = TRUE
  )

sorting_data <- sorting_data |>
  select(date, permno, exchange, ret_excess, mktcap_lag, asset_growth) |>
  filter(date > date_start + months(12))
```

The filter removes the initial year used to compute the growth rate to avoid mechanically introduced gaps from the lagging step, leaving a panel of stock-month observations with excess returns, exchange membership, lagged market capitalization, and the lagged sorting variable.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ag-percentiles
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of asset growth over time. Lines show the 33rd, 50th, and 66th percentiles of the cross-sectional distribution of asset growth in `sorting_data`, the firm-month panel used as input for portfolio construction. Asset growth is expressed as a proportion (e.g., 0.2 = 20% annual growth in total assets) and covers the full sample period of the merged CRSP-Compustat dataset."
#| echo: false
plot_data <- sorting_data |>
  drop_na() |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(
    "33%" = quantile(asset_growth, 0.33),
    "Median" = quantile(asset_growth, 0.50),
    "66%" = quantile(asset_growth, 0.66),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -date,
    names_to = "quantile",
    values_to = "asset_growth"
  )

label_data <- plot_data |>
  group_by(quantile) |>
  slice_min(abs(date - median(date)), n = 1) |>
  mutate(date = date %m+% months(36)) |> # Shift label 3 years to the right for better visibility
  ungroup()

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = date, y = asset_growth, color = quantile)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_text(
    data = label_data,
    aes(label = quantile),
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Asset growth") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

With the sorting variable constructed and merged onto the monthly stock panel, we now turn to portfolio sorts, the mechanism that translates firm-level characteristics into tradable factor returns.

### Portfolio sorts {#sec-portfolio-sorts}

In portfolio sorts, stocks are ranked each period by their sorting variable and divided into quantile portfolios. Portfolio returns are equal-weighted or value-weighted averages of constituent stock returns. The long-short factor return is the difference between the extreme portfolios, for instance bottom minus top for asset growth, reflecting the negative premium documented by @cooper.2008. Key methodological decisions include the number of portfolios, the exchange universe for computing breakpoints, the weighting scheme, and the rebalancing frequency.

The `tidyfinance` package implements this workflow through three functions. First, `breakpoint_options()` configures the sorting parameters: the number of quantile portfolios and which exchanges determine the breakpoints. Second, `compute_portfolio_returns()` takes the sorting data, applies the specified configuration, and returns portfolio-level returns. Third, `compute_long_short_returns()` constructs the hedge portfolio return from the extreme quantiles.

#### Univariate sorts {#sec-univariate-sorts}

`compute_portfolio_returns()` is built on two lower-level functions that are also available for custom workflows. `compute_breakpoints()` computes quantile cutpoints for the sorting variable from a specified exchange universe. `assign_portfolio()` maps each stock-month to a portfolio number based on those cutpoints. Researchers who need finer control, for instance to build overlapping portfolios, apply non-standard cutoffs, or weight within cells differently, can call these functions directly rather than through the high-level wrapper.

In a univariate sort, stocks are ranked on a single characteristic. We illustrate this with asset growth, forming decile portfolios using NYSE breakpoints and value-weighted returns, rebalanced annually in July.

```{r}
#| label: breakpoint-options-main
options_main <- breakpoint_options(
  n_portfolios = 5,
  breakpoint_exchanges = "NYSE"
)
```

The `breakpoint_options()` call specifies that breakpoints come from NYSE-listed stocks only, a common convention that avoids the influence of small AMEX and NASDAQ firms on portfolio cutoffs. We then pass these options to `compute_portfolio_returns()`.

```{r}
#| label: univariate-sort-ag
portfolio_returns <- compute_portfolio_returns(
  sorting_data,
  sorting_variables = "asset_growth",
  sorting_method = "univariate",
  rebalancing_month = 7,
  options_main
)
```

`compute_portfolio_returns()` returns a long tibble with one row per portfolio-month, containing value-weighted (`ret_excess_vw`), equal-weighted (`ret_excess_ew`), and capped value-weighted (`ret_excess_vw_capped`) excess returns. The long-short factor return is obtained via `compute_long_short_returns()`. The `direction = "bottom_minus_top"` argument means the factor is long low-AG stocks and short high-AG stocks, consistent with the negative premium documented by @cooper.2008.

```{r}
#| label: long-short-ag
factor_returns_ag <- portfolio_returns |>
  compute_long_short_returns(direction = "bottom_minus_top")
```

@tbl-univariate-sort-ag summarises the time series of each quintile across all three weighting schemes, with the long-short portfolio appended as the final row.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-univariate-sort-ag
#| tbl-cap: "Time-series averages of annualised monthly excess returns for asset growth quintile portfolios. Portfolios are formed annually in July using NYSE breakpoints, rebalanced annually. Means are annualised (multiplied by 12). The $t$~statistic tests whether the mean monthly excess return differs from zero. The L/S row is the long-short portfolio (bottom minus top quintile)."
#| echo: false
decile_stats <- portfolio_returns |>
  drop_na() |>
  group_by(portfolio) |>
  summarise(
    vw_mean = mean(ret_excess_vw) * 12,
    vw_tstat = mean(ret_excess_vw) / (sd(ret_excess_vw) / sqrt(n())),
    ew_mean = mean(ret_excess_ew) * 12,
    ew_tstat = mean(ret_excess_ew) / (sd(ret_excess_ew) / sqrt(n())),
    vwc_mean = mean(ret_excess_vw_capped) * 12,
    vwc_tstat = mean(ret_excess_vw_capped) /
      (sd(ret_excess_vw_capped) / sqrt(n())),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(portfolio = as.character(portfolio))

ls_row <- factor_returns_ag |>
  drop_na() |>
  summarise(
    portfolio = "L/S",
    vw_mean = mean(ret_excess_vw) * 12,
    vw_tstat = mean(ret_excess_vw) / (sd(ret_excess_vw) / sqrt(n())),
    ew_mean = mean(ret_excess_ew) * 12,
    ew_tstat = mean(ret_excess_ew) / (sd(ret_excess_ew) / sqrt(n())),
    vwc_mean = mean(ret_excess_vw_capped) * 12,
    vwc_tstat = mean(ret_excess_vw_capped) /
      (sd(ret_excess_vw_capped) / sqrt(n()))
  )

bind_rows(decile_stats, ls_row) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c(
      "Portfolio",
      "VW Mean",
      "VW t-stat",
      "EW Mean",
      "EW t-stat",
      "VWC Mean",
      "VWC t-stat"
    )
  )
```

The value-weighted long-short portfolio earns `{r} round(mean(factor_returns_ag$ret_excess_vw, na.rm=TRUE)*12*100, 1)`% per year ($t$~statistic `{r} round(mean(factor_returns_ag$ret_excess_vw, na.rm=TRUE) / (sd(factor_returns_ag$ret_excess_vw, na.rm=TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(factor_returns_ag$ret_excess_vw)))), 2)`), consistent with the negative premium documented by @cooper.2008. The equal-weighted spread is larger, as expected for characteristics that correlate with size. The monotone decline across quintiles confirms that `tidyfinance` reproduces the literature result from raw WRDS data.

#### Bivariate sorts {#sec-bivariate-sorts}

Bivariate (double) sorts control for a second variable, typically firm size (`mktcap_lag`), when forming portfolios. In dependent sorts, stocks are first sorted into groups by the secondary variable; within each group, they are then sorted on the main characteristic. In independent sorts, both sorts apply unconditionally, and portfolios form at the intersections. The factor return averages across the secondary dimension, isolating the effect of the primary variable after controlling for size. @fig-illustrate-portfolio-helper illustrates the three approaches for a single cross-section.

We reuse `options_main` from the univariate sort (five portfolios, NYSE breakpoints) and add a separate options object for the secondary size dimension:

```{r}
#| label: bivariate-sort-ag
options_secondary <- breakpoint_options(
  n_portfolios = 2,
  breakpoint_exchanges = "NYSE"
)

portfolio_returns_biv <- compute_portfolio_returns(
  sorting_data,
  c("asset_growth", "mktcap_lag"),
  sorting_method = "bivariate-dependent",
  rebalancing_month = 7,
  options_main,
  options_secondary
)

factor_returns_biv <- portfolio_returns_biv |>
  compute_long_short_returns(direction = "bottom_minus_top")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bivariate-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Univariate vs size-controlled long-short returns for asset growth. Annualized value-weighted mean excess return and $t$~statistic for the univariate sort and the dependent bivariate sort averaging across two size groups. Portfolios use NYSE breakpoints and annual July rebalancing."
#| echo: false
bind_rows(
  factor_returns_ag |>
    drop_na() |>
    summarise(
      Sort = "Univariate",
      `VW Mean` = mean(ret_excess_vw) * 12,
      `VW $t$~stat` = mean(ret_excess_vw) / (sd(ret_excess_vw) / sqrt(n()))
    ),
  factor_returns_biv |>
    drop_na() |>
    summarise(
      Sort = "Bivariate (size-controlled)",
      `VW Mean` = mean(ret_excess_vw) * 12,
      `VW $t$~stat` = mean(ret_excess_vw) / (sd(ret_excess_vw) / sqrt(n()))
    )
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, escape = TRUE)
```

The AG premium survives size control, suggesting it captures an investment effect distinct from the size factor. The `sorting_method` argument switches between dependent and independent double sorts, so researchers can inspect both configurations without modifying the pipeline.

## Factor library and API {#sec-library}

:::{.callout-note}
This section introduces the full factor library and API. 

- Explain the computation of the entire grid of factor returns across all combinations of methodological choices. Cite WWW and Gruber et al. for the motivation of this comprehensive approach. 
- Emphasise that the library is available for download, so researchers can access results without re-running the computationally intensive portfolio sort pipeline.
- Show how to download one default time series and how to use `fill_all`. 
- Illustrate Sharpe-ratio variation. 
- Mention that ´py-tidyfinance` can be used with identical callss 
::: 

### Specification grid {#sec-specification-grid}

The examples above represent single points in a high-dimensional space of methodological choices. @tbl-sorting-decisions summarises the preprocessing decisions that can be varied when constructing factor returns. The full factor library exhaustively evaluates all valid combinations of these choices for each of the sorting variables listed in @tbl-sorting-variables.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sorting-decisions
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Preprocessing choices in the portfolio sort grid and corresponding `download_data()` arguments. Italic values indicate the default. For double sorts, the secondary quantiles and exchange choices apply to the size dimension only; for univariate sorts, those rows are not applicable. FF refers to the lag procedure of @fama.1993."
tibble::tribble(
  ~`Preprocessing choice`      , ~Argument                                 , ~Options                                               , ~Description                                                                       ,
  "Size exclusion"             , "\\texttt{exclude\\_size}"                , "None; \\emph{bottom 20\\%}"                           , "Fraction of the smallest stocks (by NYSE market cap) excluded from the universe." ,
  "Exclusion of financials"    , "\\texttt{exclude\\_financials}"          , "\\emph{No}; Yes"                                      , "Drops financial-sector stocks (SIC 6000--6999) from the universe."                ,
  "Exclusion of utilities"     , "\\texttt{exclude\\_utilities}"           , "\\emph{No}; Yes"                                      , "Drops utility-sector stocks (SIC 4900--4999) from the universe."                  ,
  "Exclusion of neg. earnings" , "\\texttt{exclude\\_negative\\_earnings}" , "\\emph{No}; Yes"                                      , "Drops firms with negative earnings before sorting."                               ,
  "Sorting variable lag"       , "\\texttt{sorting\\_variable\\_lag}"      , "3m; \\emph{6m}; FF"                                   , "Lag applied to the sorting variable before portfolio assignment."                 ,
  "Rebalancing"                , "\\texttt{rebalancing}"                   , "\\emph{Monthly}; Annual"                              , "How frequently portfolios are reformed."                                          ,
  "BP: Quantiles (main)"       , "\\texttt{breakpoints\\_main}"            , "3; 5; \\emph{10}"                                     , "Number of quantile groups for the portfolio sort."                                ,
  "Sort method"                , "\\texttt{sorting\\_method}"              , "\\emph{Single}; Double dependent; Double independent" , "Single sort or sequential double sort (by size)."                                 ,
  "BP: Quantiles (secondary)"  , "\\texttt{breakpoints\\_secondary}"       , "\\emph{NA}; 2; 5"                                     , "Groups for the secondary sort variable; only relevant for double sorts."          ,
  "BP: Exchanges"              , "\\texttt{breakpoints\\_exchanges}"       , "\\emph{NYSE}; All"                                    , "Exchange(s) used to compute quantile breakpoints."                                ,
  "Weighting scheme"           , "\\texttt{weighting\\_scheme}"            , "EW; \\emph{VW}; truncated VW"                         , "Return weighting within portfolios."
) |>
  knitr::kable(
    booktabs = TRUE,
    escape = TRUE,
    col.names = c("Preprocessing choice", "Argument", "Options", "Description")
  )
```


We host precomputed factor returns for all specifications on Hugging Face and make them accessible via the `tidyfinance` API. Researchers can retrieve results without re-running the computationally intensive portfolio sort pipeline. An interactive download interface is also available at [factors.tidy-finance.org](https://factors.tidy-finance.org).


The factor library covers `{r} nrow(sorting_variable_information)` sorting variables across seven categories: investment, profitability, valuation, momentum, intangibles, trading frictions, and financing. The selection follows @jensen.2023. @tbl-sorting-variables lists all variables with their long-short direction and primary reference.

### The factor library {#sec-library-practice}

This sensitivity is not specific to AG. For all `{r} nrow(sorting_variable_information)` sorting variables in the library, construction choices shift Sharpe ratios by enough to reverse the sign of the premium for some factors. @fig-sharpe-ratio shows the distribution of annualized Sharpe ratios for each variable across all `{r} nrow(portfolio_sort_grid)` specifications.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 9
#| out-width: 100%
#| dpi: 300
#| fig-pos: p
#| fig-cap: "Sharpe ratios across construction choices. Ridge plots show the distribution of annualized Sharpe ratios of long-short return differentials for each sorting variable across all `{r} nrow(portfolio_sort_grid)` specifications illustrated in @tbl-sorting-decisions, based on the available sample period per factor. Most variables exhibit substantial variation across specifications, underscoring the sensitivity of factor returns to construction choices."
#| label: fig-sharpe-ratio
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
arrow::open_dataset(
  "data/portfolio_performance.parquet"
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sorting_variable, y = sharpe_ratio)) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(alpha = 0.3, fatten_point = 0, color = tf_dark_blue) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  guides(col = "none") +
  labs(y = "Sharpe ratio (annualized)", x = NULL) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0), linetype = "dashed") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7))
```

@fig-sharpe-ratio conveys two findings. First, most distributions are wide: construction choices have material effects on factor performance across the library. Second, for several factors the distribution spans zero, meaning the premium's sign depends on the specification. A researcher reporting a single undocumented series risks mistaking a construction artifact for an economic signal. Factors with narrow distributions centered well above zero are construction-robust; those with wide or zero-straddling distributions require sensitivity analysis before drawing conclusions.

@tbl-sorting-variables lists all `{r} nrow(sorting_variable_information)` sorting variables with their long-short direction and primary reference.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sorting-variables
#| tbl-cap: "Sorting variables in the factor library. The direction column indicates whether the long-short factor return goes long top-minus-bottom (↑) or bottom-minus-top (↓) of the characteristic distribution."
#| echo: false
tab <- sorting_variable_information |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    direction = dplyr::if_else(
      direction == "top_minus_bottom",
      "$\\uparrow$",
      "$\\downarrow$"
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(full_name) |>
  dplyr::select(sorting_variable, full_name, direction, citation) |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
    escape = FALSE,
    longtable = TRUE,
    col.names = c("Variable", "Name", "", "Main reference")
  )

tab[1] <- sub("llll", "lp{5cm}ll", tab[1], fixed = TRUE)
tab
```

To download factor returns from the factor library, call
```{r}
#| label: download-factor-library
asset_growth_returns <- download_data(
  "tidyfinance",
  "factor_library",
  sorting_variable = "ag",
  sorting_variable_lag = "6m"
)
```

The defaults passed to `dataset = "factor_library"` reflect one common construction choice but may not suit every research question. Always verify that the selected combination matches the intended design before drawing conclusions.

```{r}
#| label: download-factor-library-fill-all
#| eval: false
download_data(
  "tidyfinance",
  "factor_library",
  sorting_variable = "52w",
  sorting_variable_lag = "6m",
  fill_all = TRUE
)
```

For finer control, `tidyfinance` exposes lower-level helpers that sit beneath the `download_data()` interface. `get_available_huggingface_files()` returns all available files for a given Hugging Face repository as a tibble; `download_factor_library_returns_ids()` retrieves returns for a specific vector of precomputed specification IDs. Researchers who want to iterate over a custom subset of specifications rather than filter by parameter value will prefer this route.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| label: download-factor-library-ids
full_grid <- get_available_huggingface_files(
  "tidy-finance",
  "factor-library-grid"
) |>
  dplyr::pull(.data$url) |>
  arrow::read_parquet()

tidyfinance:::download_factor_library_ids(123)
```

## Summary and discussion {#sec-summary}

::: {.callout-note}
Keep brief or delete entirely, as the main paper's conclusion already covers the key points.
::: 

Factor returns encode their construction history. Two researchers following the same paper can produce different factor series, with no way of knowing why, because breakpoints, weighting, and lagging conventions are rarely published alongside the data. `tidyfinance` 
makes these decisions visible: the package covers `{r} nrow(sorting_variable_information)` 
sorting variables across `{r} nrow(portfolio_sort_grid)` documented specifications, each reproducible from raw WRDS and Compustat data in a single, version-controlled workflow.

The library currently covers US equities. Construction-choice sensitivity in international markets is beyond its current scope.

The broader implication is methodological. Researchers who disagree about a construction choice can resolve the disagreement empirically: run both variants through the same pipeline, compare factor returns, and report the difference. The API and interactive dashboard extend this accessibility to practitioners who need standardized series without running the full pipeline.

With `{r} nrow(portfolio_sort_grid)` specifications across `{r} nrow(sorting_variable_information)` sorting variables, the library makes systematic sensitivity analysis newly tractable. This opens a path toward meta-analytic evidence on which factor properties are robust and which are artifacts of undocumented defaults.
